data.content:
Forward Edge Of The Battle Area
The foremost limits of a series of areas where ground combat units are deployed, marking the planned limit for direct fire effects.

Class V
A category of supplies consisting of ammunition required for battle positions.

Direct Fire Control Measures
Measures used by commanders to control fires, including target reference points and trigger lines.<SEP>Measures established by headquarters to control direct fire during linkup operations.

Final Protective Fire
An immediately available, prearranged barrier of fire designed to impede enemy movement across defensive lines or areas.

Forward Line Of Own Troops
A line indicating the most forward positions of friendly forces in any kind of military operation at a specific time.

Platoon
A military unit size considered too small to secure a perimeter for a strong point.

Company
A military unit size that normally occupies strong points.

Trigger Lines
A specific type of direct fire control measure used to control engagement.

Battalion
A military unit size that normally occupies strong points.<SEP>A military unit echelon for which defending an AO is a typical mission.

FSCLs
Fire Support Coordination Lines, identified as a type of permissive fire support coordination measure.

Brigade
A military unit size that may construct strong points.

Squad
A military unit size considered too small to secure a perimeter for a strong point.

Free-Fire Area
A permissive fire support coordination measure where weapons may be fired without coordination.

Coordinated Fire Line
A permissive fire support coordination measure used to control indirect fires.

Airspace Coordination Area
A restrictive fire support coordination measure used to coordinate airspace usage.

Friendly Fire Incidents
Unintentional firing on friendly forces, which restrictive fire support coordination measures aim to prevent.<SEP>Risk increased by unique characteristics of shantytowns such as narrow pathways and weapon penetration.<SEP>Friendly fire incidents are critical to prevent through positive identification of friendly positions.

No Fire Area
A restrictive fire support coordination measure where fires are prohibited.

Fire Support Chain
The fire support chain includes observers and cells that must understand the commander's intent to execute the scheme of maneuver.

MBA
The Main Battle Area where enemy forces attempt to break through defending units.<SEP>The MBA, or Main Battle Area, is the location where a defending force is less effective if an attacking enemy force deploys there.

FSCMs
Fire Support Coordination Measures are placed by commanders to enable the rapid engagement of attacking enemy forces.<SEP>Fire Support Coordination Measures established by headquarters to control fire support during linkup operations.

Fire Support Assets
Fire support assets target enemy combat units to force deployment, inflict casualties, and disrupt the cohesion of attacks.

FPFs
Final Protective Fires are priority targets designated for artillery units and mortar platoons during defensive operations.

Artillery Units
Artillery units are supporting units that can be assigned a single FPF and are laid on targets when not engaged in other missions.

Indirect and Joint Fires
Indirect and joint fires are employed by a defending force to attack enemy forces in vulnerable locations.

Mortar Platoons
Mortar platoons are supporting units designated to conduct defensive operations and assigned FPFs.

Joint Force Commander
The Joint Force Commander seeks to gain and maintain air superiority to allow friendly forces to operate without prohibitive interference.<SEP>The Joint Force Commander receives working knowledge of critical infrastructure from Army special operations forces.

Army Air Defense Artillery Forces
Army air defense artillery forces operate interdependently to provide air and missile defense and protect high-value assets.

Aerial Threats
Aerial threats are enemy dangers that air defense artillery forces aim to deter or defeat to protect the force.

Air Superiority
Air superiority is a condition required by the Joint Force Commander to ensure freedom of operation for friendly forces.

Ground Commanders
Ground commanders mitigate the risk of air and missile attack through various activities to improve unit survivability.

Camouflage
Camouflage is an activity used by ground commanders to reduce the likelihood of detection from the air.

Ammunition
Ammunition is a priority item for replenishment in the defensive plan and may be stockpiled within the MBA.

Obstacle Plan
The Obstacle Plan is a tactical plan that the fire support chain must understand to distribute fire effects.

Denial Operations
Denial operations involve plans to destroy stockpiled ammunition and supplies if necessary during a defense.<SEP>Operations where commanders plan to destroy stocks if necessary to prevent enemy use.<SEP>Operations conducted by designated units during retrograde movements to delay or disrupt enemy forces.

Final Protective Line
A Final Protective Line is a predetermined line assigned to a direct fire weapon system as a form of Final Protective Fires.

High-Value Assets
High-Value Assets are critical resources protected by Army air defense artillery forces during operations.

Early Warning
Early Warning is information disseminated to units to improve survivability by predicting impact points and detecting launches.<SEP>Alerts provided to a protected force regarding enemy activity, the primary output of screen operations.

Direct Fire Systems
Direct Fire Systems are weapons that engage enemy forces canalized by obstacles and fire support coverage.

Sustainment Unit Commanders
Commanders who understand the supported commander’s intent and establish support priorities for sustainment operations.<SEP>Sustainment Unit Commanders understand the supported commander's intent and establish support priorities.

Defensive Counterair Support
A type of support that commanders may request to defend against enemy air threats.

Enemy Insertion
The act of enemy forces placing troops or equipment into an area, which defending forces attempt to detect and counter.

Drop Zone
A specific area identified by the IPB process where enemy forces are expected to parachute personnel or supplies.<SEP>A designated area where troops or supplies are dropped by parachute, subject to risk prioritization and surveillance by commanders.

Joint Offensive Counterair Support
A type of support that commanders may request to counter enemy air threats offensively.

Fire Support Plan
A plan that includes target lists for drop and landing zones to cover potential enemy insertion areas.<SEP>A plan that includes drop and landing zones in its target list for area fires and scatterable munitions.

Area Fires Munitions
Munitions included in the fire support plan to target specific zones.

Scatterable Munitions
Munitions deployed over a wide area, included in the fire support plan for drop and landing zones.

High-Payoff Targets
High-Payoff Targets are specific targets that friendly forces aim to destroy or neutralize without wasting assets.

Critical Friendly Installation
Key facilities or sites that defending forces protect through countermobility and survivability efforts.

Landing Zone
A specific area identified by the IPB process where enemy forces are expected to land aircraft for air assault operations.<SEP>A designated area where aircraft can land, subject to risk prioritization, surveillance, and targeting by defending forces.

Attack Helicopter
An armed aircraft used to quickly engage enemy forces concentrated in landing and drop zones.

Base Cluster Defense
A defensive force responsible for keeping enemy forces under observation and designating targets.

Quick Response Force
A rapidly deployable unit that fixes enemy forces to allow a tactical combat force to counterattack.

Joint Fires
Fires employed against enemy insertion areas using assets from two or more components.

Target Acquisition Optic
Devices used by enemy forces for targeting, the use of which can be denied by obscurants.

Tactical Combat Force
A unit committed to counterattack enemy forces that have landed and consolidated.<SEP>A tactical combat force is a unit that responds to Level III threats after military police maintain contact.

Thermal Sight
A mechanical aid capable of overcoming or partially overcoming darkness.

Intelligence Officer
A staff member who coordinates the development of a synchronized information collection plan.

Intelligence Product
Analysis used by commanders to identify probable enemy objectives, approaches, and vulnerabilities.

Information Collection Plan
A synchronized and integrated plan developed to satisfy maneuver, targeting, and information requirements.<SEP>The information collection plan is the overall strategy into which commanders integrate CBRN reconnaissance and surveillance.

Named Area Of Interest
A specific area identified by commanders during planning to focus intelligence collection efforts.

Targeted Area Of Interest
A specific area identified by commanders, often developed from probable enemy objectives and approaches.

Information Collection Asset
Resources used to gather intelligence, which require sustainment and protection due to susceptibility to loss.

IPB
Intelligence Preparation of the Battlefield, a process used to determine enemy strength, courses of action, and vulnerabilities.

Enemy Follow-on Force
Reinforcement units that arrive after the initial enemy assault, whose location and commitment time are analyzed.

Response Force
A military unit that, along with base cluster defense, keeps enemy forces under observation and designates targets for available fires.

Army Indirect Fire
Fires delivered by Army assets not in direct line of sight of the target, used to neutralize or destroy enemy forces.

Staff
Personnel who support commanders by rapidly transmitting coordination decisions to all concerned.<SEP>The group with whom intelligence officers coordinate to develop a synchronized information collection plan.

Mechanical Aid
Equipment such as thermal sights that can overcome or partially overcome limited visibility conditions like darkness.

Darkness
A limited visibility condition that mechanical aids can overcome or partially overcome.

Sensor
Devices that may retain value in limited visibility conditions where mechanical aids are ineffective.

Air Avenue Of Approach
A route through the airspace used by forces, which obscurants can deny the enemy from using.

Visual Navigation Aid
Tools used for navigation that obscurants can deny an enemy force from using.

Cover And Concealment
A military aspect of terrain used for protection from enemy observation and fire, determined by commanders.

Cyberspace Activity
Operations in cyberspace identified by IPB products regarding enemy forces.

Defensive Plan
A plan that must address the sustainment, replacement, and reconstitution of information collection assets.

Observation
A military aspect of terrain that commanders determine to assess visibility and fields of view.

Field Of Fire
A military aspect of terrain referring to the area a weapon can cover effectively, determined by commanders.

Attack Using Uncommitted Forces
The preferred method for transitioning to the offense using forces from the reserve or reinforcements not previously committed to defense.

Reinforcements
Additional military forces that arrive to support operations, capable of conducting attacks without prior combat fatigue.

Attack Using Defending Forces
A method for transitioning to the offense using forces currently engaged in defense, offering speed and surprise.

Units In Contact
Military forces currently engaged with the enemy that must be retained to fix enemy forces during an attack.

Subordinate Units
Military units under a commander's control that are reinforced to execute an attack or maintain defense.

Negotiated End To Hostilities
A diplomatic resolution that may trigger a transition from defensive operations to stability operations.

Reserve Assembly Areas
Locations where reserve forces gather, requiring an approach or tactical road march to reach the front lines.

CBRN Hazards
CBRN hazards are threats analyzed using Mission-oriented protective posture analysis to determine appropriate protective measures.<SEP>CBRN hazards are threats from chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear sources against which defending units are vulnerable.

CBRN Personnel
CBRN personnel contribute to unit protection, perform vulnerability assessments, and recommend vulnerability reduction measures.

AOs
Areas of Operation prepared by defending units before attacking enemy forces arrive or established behind a security force.<SEP>Areas of Operations from which reinforcements may move to join the engagement.

CBRN Vulnerability Assessment
CBRN vulnerability assessments include threat assessment and vulnerability analysis to provide preventive measures for CBRN defense.

Mission-oriented Protective Posture
Mission-oriented protective posture (MOPP) is a method used to determine protective posture and estimate unit effectiveness against hazards.

MOPP Analysis
MOPP analysis is a tool used to determine appropriate protective posture and estimate logistic requirements during CBRN threats.<SEP>MOPP analysis is a tool used to support determining protective posture, estimating logistic requirements, and assessing tradeoffs between agent exposure and performance.

Physical Security
Physical security is an operation that commanders prioritize throughout a defense, especially during noncontiguous operations.

Antiterrorism
Antiterrorism involves operations that commanders monitor throughout a defense to protect against enemy attacks indistinguishable from terrorist acts.

Military Police Elements
Military police elements support defending units by enhancing physical security and antiterrorism capabilities within an echelon support area.

Dislocated Civilians
Dislocated civilians are populations that affect the defense and are managed using host-nation and international organizations to minimize disaster effects.

Population And Resource Control
Population and resource control measures are planned by commanders to manage dislocated civilians and minimize effects on the defense.

Level III Threats
Level III threats are security risks that military police maintain contact with until a tactical combat force responds.

Encircled Force
An encircled force is a military unit surrounded by enemy forces, often conducting a breakout or exfiltration to survive.

Civil Affairs Units
Civil affairs units assist commanders in planning population and resource control measures during defensive operations.<SEP>Civil Affairs Units conduct operations to leverage civilian capabilities and support partner government recovery.<SEP>Civil Affairs Units work with civilian authorities and Army protection units to reestablish civil control, essential services, and coordinate populace and resources control measures.<SEP>Partner with critical civil networks to rapidly reconstitute partner governance capacity.

Breakout
A breakout is an operation conducted by an encircled force to regain freedom of movement or contact with friendly units.

Exfiltration
Exfiltration is an organized method to preserve a portion of a force if a breakout fails or is questionable.

Enemy Supply Stocks
Enemy supply stocks are resources that an isolated unit may use to sustain itself while attacking deeper.

Seizure Of Key Terrain
Seizure of key terrain is a risky course of action where an encircled force attacks deeper into enemy territory.

Friendly Ground Forces
Friendly ground forces are military units that meet during a linkup operation.<SEP>Military units that conduct linkups, advance on objectives, or engage in defensive and offensive operations against enemy forces.

Medical Personnel
Medical personnel continuously maintain and conduct comprehensive health surveillance including medical, occupational, and environmental aspects.<SEP>Trained individuals who advise the commander on whether to use MEDEVAC and CASEVAC.

Linkup
A linkup is a meeting of friendly ground forces occurring in various circumstances, such as after a breakout.<SEP>A meeting of friendly ground forces occurring in various circumstances, such as when an advancing force reaches an objective or an encircled element breaks out.

Level II Threats
Level II threats are security risks that military police may defeat against bases and base clusters located in an echelon support area.

Conventional Reconnaissance Assets
Conventional reconnaissance assets are existing capabilities whose efforts should not be duplicated by CBRN reconnaissance and surveillance.

Civilian Population Centers
Civilian population centers are locations attacked by enemy forces in an attempt to disrupt the defense.

Health Surveillance
Health surveillance is a comprehensive activity conducted by medical personnel to monitor health and environmental conditions.

CBRN Passive Defense Training
CBRN passive defense training is a responsibility of commanders to prepare units to respond properly to CBRN threats.

Vulnerability Reduction Measures
Vulnerability reduction measures are recommendations provided by CBRN personnel to commanders to enhance protection before and after moving into defensive positions.

Perimeter
The perimeter is the area where an encircled force must maintain a simultaneous defense during a breakout operation.

Support Area
An area where terrain management is critical for establishing bases and base clusters.<SEP>The support area is a zone that must be protected from enemy attacks to ensure the success of a unit defense.

International Organizations
International organizations are entities used by defending units to minimize the effects of disaster or conflict on dislocated civilians.<SEP>International Organizations are entities with which Army special operations forces develop enduring partnerships.

Enemy Rear Area
The enemy rear area is a location where an encircled friendly force may attack to disrupt the enemy's offense.

Flexibility
A characteristic of the defense requiring plans that anticipate enemy actions and allow for shifting the main effort and allocating resources.

Disruption
A characteristic of the defense involving actions to desynchronize enemy preparations, isolate forward echelons, and target command and control systems.

Maneuver
A characteristic of the defense that allows a force to achieve and exploit a position of advantage using static and mobile elements.

Operations in Depth
The simultaneous application of combat power throughout an area of operations to disrupt enemy capabilities and prevent early successes.

Mass and Concentration
A characteristic of the defense involving the production of overwhelming combat power at specific locations to support decisive operations.

Preparation
A characteristic of the defense involving the occupation and improvement of positions, study of terrain, and preparation of engagement areas before contact.

Security
A characteristic of the defense utilizing security forces to protect defending forces from surprise and reduce unknowns.<SEP>An enabling operation discussed in the context of military actions.

Command and Control Systems
Enemy systems targeted by defending forces to disrupt operations in depth.

Combined Arms
The synchronization of different military arms, which disruption actions aim to impede.

Engagement Areas
Engagement Areas are designated locations where defending forces combine obstacles and fires to destroy or canalize enemy forces.<SEP>Specific areas prepared by defending forces to intercept and engage the enemy.<SEP>Designated zones where defending forces integrate direct and indirect fires to defeat enemy attacks.<SEP>Designated locations where units concentrate fires to destroy or degrade the enemy in an area defense.

Defending Forces
Defending Forces are units that prepare their areas of operation before enemy forces arrive, establishing defenses, studying terrain, and preparing engagement areas.<SEP>The specific military units conducting defensive operations, improving positions, and maneuvering against the enemy.

Mutual Support
Mutual support exists when positions and units support each other by direct and indirect fires, preventing enemy forces from attacking one position without being subjected to fire from adjacent positions.<SEP>A tactical condition where positions support each other by direct and indirect fires to strengthen defenses and prevent infiltration.

Tactical Obstacle
A type of reinforcing obstacle designed to shape enemy maneuver, maximize the effects of fires, and affect the tempo of operations.

Protective Obstacle
A type of reinforcing obstacle employed to protect personnel, equipment, supplies, and facilities against threats in defensive or security roles.

Reinforcing Obstacle
Artificial obstacles constructed or emplaced to augment existing natural obstacles, categorized as either tactical or protective.

Reserved Obstacle
A specific obstacle for which the commander retains execution authority to allow coordination with other battlefield activities.

Fire
The use of weapon systems to create lethal effects, integrated with obstacles to enhance their effectiveness and canalize enemy movement.

data.content:
Enemy Airborne and Air Assault Attack
An offensive operation involving enemy forces utilizing vertical envelopment via drop zones or landing zones.

Vertical Envelopment
A maneuver tactic where enemy forces bypass defensive lines by air, using drop zones or landing zones to insert troops.

CBRN Reconnaissance Systems
Systems used to mark contaminated and clean routes, contributing to mobility in contaminated environments.

Pickup Zone
A location identified by intelligence processes where enemy forces load for air movement.

Airfield
A location identified by intelligence processes from which enemy forces launch airborne operations.<SEP>A suitable landing area under friendly control required for fixed-wing aircraft operations in the urban environment.

Unit Leader
A leader responsible for coordinating the nature and extent of mutual support within a defensive position.

Obstacle Zone
A designated area where commanders authorize the placement of obstacles.

Scatterable Mine
A type of mine with specific firing and self-destruct times used to create obstacles.

Obstacle Belt
A designated area for obstacles, tracked by commanders during defensive preparations.

Directed Obstacle
A type of tactical obstacle whose employment is directed by a higher authority.

Stocks
Materials that commanders plan to destroy if necessary as part of denial operations.

Situational Obstacle
A type of tactical obstacle employed based on specific battlefield conditions.

Obstacle Materials
Materials used in a defense that require detailed coordination and long lead times for supply.

Sustainment Staff Officers
Officers who plan sustainment operations in accordance with the commander's intent.

Sustainment Operations
Operations planned to ensure support for the overall defensive operation, including branches and sequels.

Sustainment Unit
Units positioned in bases or base clusters to fulfill support tasks and maintain security.

Resupply Vehicles
Vehicles that may need to be infiltrated to reduce detection chances when the enemy possesses significant surveillance capability.

Combat-Configured Loads
Packages tailored to a specific unit size, containing water, CBRN supplies, barrier materials, ammunition, POL, medical supplies, and repair parts.

POL
Petroleum, oil, and lubricants included as part of combat-configured loads.

CBRN Defense Supplies
Supplies for chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear defense included in combat-configured loads.

Base Clusters
Clusters where sustainment units are positioned for security and to avoid interrupting sustainment functions.

Terrain Management
A critical consideration when establishing bases and base clusters in the support area.

Maintenance Collection Points
Points where maintenance support is provided as far forward as possible to reduce equipment evacuation needs.

Medical Support
Support that anticipates significant casualties and plans for mass casualty situations and evacuation.

Base and Base Cluster Commanders
Commanders designated by the support area commander to be responsible for the local security of their respective bases.

Enemy Reconnaissance Efforts
Efforts by enemy forces that security operations aim to deter, detect, or defeat.

Support Area Commander
The individual responsible for defensive planning, risk mitigation, and coordinating security in the support area.<SEP>The support area commander coordinates to mitigate the effects of performing security operations on the primary functions of units located within an echelon support area.

Weapon Systems
Damaged systems that maintenance personnel aim to repair and return to a unit in combat-ready condition.

ATP 3-91
A manual discussing the use of bases and base clusters within the division support area.

ADP 3-37
A manual providing additional information on protection.

Multifunctional Forward Logistic Elements
Units containing maintenance personnel and equipment designed to rapidly repair weapon systems as far forward as possible.

Obscurants
Materials used by commanders to help conceal logistic operations from enemy detection.

Cached Commodities
Supplies stored in hidden locations that commanders protect during security operations.

Medical Corps Officers
Officers specifically excluded from being designated as base and base cluster commanders.

Ambulance Exchange Points
Designated locations included in evacuation plans for transferring casualties.<SEP>Points planned for establishment to facilitate casualty evacuation in urban areas.<SEP>Marked locations for transferring casualties, included in operational graphics for MEDEVAC and CASEVAC crews.

Combat Trains
Elements whose movement commanders secure during security operations in a defense.

Tenant Units
Units located within a support area whose commanders may be designated as base and base cluster commanders.

Resupply Convoys
Resupply convoys are critical operations that require security planning and coordination.

ATP 3-37.10
ATP 3-37.10 is a reference document detailing the strengths and weaknesses of dispersed and consolidated approaches for arraying base camps.<SEP>A publication referenced for its discussion on the strengths and weaknesses of dispersed and consolidated approaches for arraying base camps.

Base Camps
Camps that can be arrayed using either dispersed or consolidated approaches.

Sustainment Units
Sustainment units support the operations of maneuver and other forces, though their ability to accomplish primary missions may be impacted by higher protection standards.

Troop Movements
Troop movements are critical operations requiring staffs to balance terrain management, movement planning, and traffic-circulation control.<SEP>Movements over extended distances that require significant sustainment requirements.

Military Police
Military police protect movements, prevent congestion, respond to maneuver plan changes, and provide convoy escorts.

Main Supply Routes
Main supply routes are routes maintained by mobility resources to support the forward movement of units and supplies and the rearward evacuation of personnel and equipment.

Survivability Operations
Survivability operations involve actions taken by a defending commander to reduce the risk of losses from enemy attacks, including hardening positions and using cover.

Survivability Plan
A survivability plan is developed by a defending commander to reduce the risk of losses through various protective measures.

Survivability Positions
Survivability positions are constructed locations such as trenches, command post shelters, and fighting positions designed to protect personnel and equipment.

Army Maneuver Enhancement Brigade
An Army maneuver enhancement brigade is a higher headquarters unit that supports divisions or corps when BCT engineer capabilities are exceeded.

Engineer Units
Engineer units assist maneuver and supporting units in preparing survivability positions and field fortifications.

Cover
Cover is a method of protection utilizing natural terrain features like folds in the earth and trees, or constructed fortifications like digging in.<SEP>A type of security operation conducted independently to protect the main body by fighting to gain time and preventing enemy observation.

BCT Engineer Battalions
BCT engineer battalions possess specific capabilities for engineer support, though requirements beyond their capabilities are passed to higher headquarters.

Dispersion
Dispersion is a defensive technique used to limit damage from enemy attacks by spreading out unit personnel and equipment.

CBRN Defense
CBRN defense involves plans and measures established to protect personnel and equipment from chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear hazards.

Transportation Units
Transportation units are military organizations that can, in some circumstances, provide their own security for movements.

Concealment
Concealment is a method used by units to enhance survivability by avoiding detection and destruction by enemy forces.

Subordinates
Personnel who exercise disciplined initiative and adjust to new situations to achieve the commander's intent.

Disciplined Initiative
Action taken by subordinates in the absence of orders to react to unforeseen enemy actions or opportunities.

Commanders Intent
A command and control principle that defines the limits within which subordinates may exercise initiative and provides confidence in ambiguous situations.

Shaping Operations
Operations conducted to contain enemy attacks until the defending force can seize the initiative.<SEP>Operations conducted to attrit, disrupt, and delay the enemy to establish conditions for decisive operations.<SEP>Operations consisting of enabling operations conducted by commanders to create conditions for decisive operations.

Control Measures
Measures such as contact points and phase lines used to coordinate flank and rear activities.

Defending Commander
A commander conducting a defensive mission who allocates resources, shifts efforts, and manages reserves.

Defensive Mission
A military assignment that generally imposes few restrictions on a defending commander while requiring prevention of enemy penetration.

Task Organization
The arrangement of forces and resources to respond to existing or projected situations.

Defensive Positions
Locations occupied by defending forces to engage attackers, often reinforced by obstacles.<SEP>Locations occupied by units that achieve mutual support through observation, fires, and patrol activities.

Command Posts
Static facilities placed in hardened terrain to reduce electronic and visual signatures.

Standard Operating Procedures
Established procedures employed by elements of a task-organized unit to ensure understanding and synchronization.<SEP>Established procedures required to obtain proficiency in the conduct of security operations.

Counterattacks
Offensive actions taken by a defending unit to restore defensive integrity if a position is overrun.<SEP>Offensive actions conducted to regain the initiative or destroy enemy forces after an enemy success.

COA
Course of Action; disciplined initiative may offer a greater chance of success than the original COA.

Communications Nodes
Facilities that tend to be relatively static in the defense and are placed in hardened areas to reduce signatures.

Battlefield
The area of conflict which commanders may shape by defending in one area and delaying in another.

Common Operational Picture
A shared display of relevant information established by headquarters to coordinate operations and situational awareness.

Retrograde Operations
Operations conducted when a defense is unsuccessful, allowing a force to preserve combat capability and establish conditions for future success.

Mobile Defense
Mobile Defense is a type of defensive operation that concentrates on the destruction or defeat of the enemy through a decisive attack by a striking force.<SEP>A defensive method relying on a striking force to generate overwhelming combat power at a decisive point.<SEP>A type of defense where transitioning to the offense generally follows a striking force's attack.

Striking Force
A Striking Force is a dedicated counterattack force in a mobile defense constituted with the bulk of available combat power.<SEP>A decisive force used in mobile defense to generate overwhelming combat power against the enemy.<SEP>A designated unit used in a mobile defense whose attack typically precedes the transition to offensive operations.

Window Of Opportunity
A timeframe identified by a defending commander to transition to the offense when the enemy is overextended.

Soviets
The Soviets are a military force that conducted an area defense during the Battle of Kursk in July 1943.

Recognition Signals
Signals established by headquarters to ensure positive identification between converging forces during a linkup.

German General Manstein
German General Manstein is a historical military leader who conducted a mobile defense during the Donbas Operation.

Communication Procedures
Procedures established by headquarters to coordinate radio traffic and information exchange during linkup operations.

Battle of Kursk
The Battle of Kursk is a historical event in July 1943 that serves as an example of an area defense conducted by the Soviets.

Fixing Force
A Fixing Force is a designated unit that supplements the striking force by preventing the enemy from moving from a specific area and canalizing them into ambush areas.

Donbas Operation
The Donbas Operation is a historical military operation in Ukraine in February 1943 that serves as an example of a mobile defense.

Ukraine
Ukraine is the geographical location where the Donbas Operation took place in February 1943.<SEP>Country that received military assistance and transformed its special operations capabilities.

Withdrawal
Withdrawal is a variation of retrograde where a force disengages from an enemy force and moves in a direction away from the enemy.

Armored and Stryker Forces
Military units equipped with armored combat vehicles that utilize tactical mobility and protection for defense and security operations.

Survivability Move
A tactical method involving the rapid displacement of a unit, command post, or facility in response to direct and indirect fires, threats, or intelligence.

Airborne and Air Assault Units
Infantry forces deployed via landing zones, often suited for reserve roles, rapid reinforcement, and flank protection.

Spoiling Attacks
A preemptive offensive operation conducted to disrupt enemy troop concentrations and attack preparations before an offensive can be launched.

Armored Combat Vehicles
Vehicles that provide tactical mobility, protection, and the capability to maneuver in dynamic and static defenses.

Aviation Forces
Units utilizing a mix of manned and unmanned systems for reconnaissance, security, shaping operations, and counterattacks.

Manned and Unmanned Systems
Systems operated by aviation forces to provide speed, mobility, and versatility in defense operations.

Command and Control Capabilities
Critical enemy functions that allow direction of forces, targeted for degradation by the defending force to compel culmination.

Road Network
Transportation infrastructure that influences maneuver; limited networks confine the enemy, while good networks facilitate friendly repositioning.

Integrated Fires Complex
A coordinated enemy system of firepower targeted for destruction or degradation by the defending force.

Economy of Force
A principle or measure where commanders allocate minimum essential combat power to secondary areas to focus on the decisive operation.

Minefields
Explosive obstacles employed by aviation forces to assist in the countermobility effort against enemy forces.

Natural Object
A strong point is often tied to a natural or reinforcing obstacle to enhance defense.

Fire Support Systems
Fire support systems cover barriers and gaps to provide better targets for direct fire systems.

Host-nation Organizations
Host-nation organizations are used to minimize the effects of conflict on dislocated civilians.

Enabling Operations
Operations discussed in Chapter 5, including reconnaissance, security, troop movement, relief in place, and passage of lines, which support decisive action.

Troop Movement
An enabling operation discussed in Chapter 5.<SEP>The movement of soldiers and units from one place to another by any available means to posture forces for operations.

FM 3-13
A publication that discusses information operations.<SEP>A military publication referenced in the text defining information warfare.

Passage of Lines
An enabling operation discussed in Chapter 5.<SEP>An operation where a force moves forward or rearward through another force's combat positions.

Relief in Place
An enabling operation discussed in Chapter 5.<SEP>An operation in which a unit is replaced by an incoming unit, transferring mission responsibilities.

Mobility Operations
An enabling operation discussed in ATP 3-90.4.

Countermobility Operations
An enabling operation discussed in ATP 3-90.8.

Decisive Action
A category of military operations to which enabling operations apply.

Fundamentals of Successful Reconnaissance
A set of seven principles guiding commanders in conducting effective reconnaissance.

Reconnaissance in Force
A type of reconnaissance operation designed to discover or test enemy strength, dispositions, and reactions.

Area Reconnaissance
A type of reconnaissance operation focused on obtaining detailed information about terrain or enemy activity within a prescribed area.

Route Reconnaissance
A type of reconnaissance operation to obtain detailed information of a specified route and all terrain from which the enemy could influence movement.

Zone Reconnaissance
A type of reconnaissance operation to obtain detailed information on routes, obstacles, terrain, and enemy forces within a zone defined by boundaries.<SEP>A type of reconnaissance operation involving a directed effort to obtain detailed information on routes, obstacles, terrain, and enemy forces within a specific zone.

JP 2-0
A joint publication that provides the definition of reconnaissance.

Special Reconnaissance
Reconnaissance and surveillance actions conducted in hostile or sensitive environments to collect information of strategic or operational significance.<SEP>Method conducted in the extended deep area to reinforce commanders ability to locate and interdict enemy capabilities.

Special Forces
Units specifically trained to conduct reconnaissance operations.<SEP>Units involved in foreign internal defense activities during competition.<SEP>Future units resembling Detachment 101 capabilities, mentioned alongside Civil Affairs.

JP 3-05
A joint publication that defines special reconnaissance.<SEP>JP 3-05 provides definitions regarding denied areas and operational constraints.<SEP>Joint Publication referenced regarding operational constraints and force capabilities in the extended deep area.

Ground Cavalry
Units specifically trained to conduct reconnaissance operations.

Aviation Attack Reconnaissance Units
Units specifically trained to conduct reconnaissance operations.

Scouts
Personnel specifically trained to conduct reconnaissance operations.

Corps of Engineers
A branch that conducts specific reconnaissance operations to complement the overall effort.

Chemical Corps
A branch that conducts specific reconnaissance operations.

BCT
Brigade Combat Team commanders who use organic or attached reconnaissance and intelligence elements.

Defense Support of Civil Authorities
Tasks supported by enabling operations, directed by commanders.

Priority Information Requirements
Requirements that result from the IPB process and serve as the basis for assigning reconnaissance objectives.

Supporting Efforts
Activities where enabling operations are usually conducted by commanders.

Courses of Action
Potential strategies formulated, confirmed, or modified using information from the IPB process.

Governmental Agencies
Agencies that observe and report civilian, adversary, and enemy activity in support and consolidation areas.

CBRN Contamination
Areas affected by Chemical, Biological, Radiological, or Nuclear hazards, considered obstacles during reconnaissance.<SEP>Chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear contamination considered an obstacle during zone reconnaissance.

Reinforcement
A planned action for a friendly force during reconnaissance in force.

Small Units
Units that conduct reconnaissance relying primarily on the human dynamic rather than technical means.

Area Security
A type of security operation conducted to protect friendly forces, lines of communications, and activities within a specific area.<SEP>Area security is the responsibility of the land component commander including rear area protection.

Dismounted Marches
A method of troop movement where soldiers move on foot.

Screen
A type of security operation that primarily provides early warning to the protected force.

Army BCT
Army Brigade Combat Teams, including armored, infantry, and Stryker types, capable of conducting security operations.

Administrative Movement
A type of troop movement arranged to expedite movement and conserve time and energy when no enemy interference is anticipated.

Approach March
The advance of a combat unit when direct contact with the enemy is intended, emphasizing speed over tactical deployment.

FM 3-90-2
A field manual providing additional information on the conduct of security operations.<SEP>A field manual providing additional information on the conduct of relief in place and passage of lines.

Guard
A type of security operation conducted to protect the main body by fighting, relying on the main body's support and unable to operate independently.

Tactical Road March
A rapid movement used to relocate units within an area of operations to prepare for combat operations.

FM 4-01
A field manual discussing Army transportation operations and various transportation modes.<SEP>A field manual discussing various transportation modes related to movement.

Mounted Marches
A method of troop movement using vehicles.

Forced March
A method to hurry dismounted or mounted marches over extended distances when necessary.<SEP>A hurried dismounted or mounted march conducted when necessary.

Echelon Logistic Staff Officer
The staff officer responsible for supervising administrative movements.

FM 3-98
A field manual providing additional information on the conduct of security operations.

ATP 4-01.45
An Army techniques publication discussing tactical convoy operations.

Friendly Force
A military force or unit that security operations aim to protect from surprise and enemy interference.<SEP>Friendly Force refers to allied military units requiring protection and identification during operations.

Civilian Population
Non-military personnel within an area of operations who may be protected by security forces.<SEP>Noncombatants in the urban area who are affected by the impassability of destroyed road surfaces.<SEP>The Civilian Population in urban environments affects PID, CD, and ROE assessments and increases risks.

Infantry BCT
Infantry Brigade Combat Team, a type of Army BCT capable of conducting security operations and tactical marches.

Battlefield Agility
The capability to conduct rapid and orderly movement to concentrate combat power at decisive points.

Relieved Unit
A unit that is replaced in an area during a relief in place operation.

Movement Control
The dual process of committing allocated transportation assets and regulating movements to synchronize distribution flow.

Land Forces
Forces that are sustained by the synchronization of distribution flow over lines of communications.

Incoming Unit
A unit that replaces another unit and assumes responsibility for the mission and assigned zone of operations.

Deliberate Relief in Place
A relief in place characterized by in-depth planning and preparation.

Zone of Operations
An area assigned to a unit, a term used in joint doctrine, which the Army refers to as an Area of Operations.

JP 3-07.3
A joint publication referenced for the definition of relief in place.

Sequential Relief in Place
A type of relief in place where elements are relieved in succession based on deployment.

Staggered Relief in Place
A type of relief in place where elements are relieved in a sequence determined by the tactical situation.

Rearward Passage of Lines
A passage of lines occurring when a unit passes through another unit's positions while moving away from the enemy.

Simultaneous Relief in Place
A type of relief in place where all elements are relieved at the same time, taking the least time to execute.

Hasty Relief in Place
A relief in place conducted with limited planning and preparation time.

Passing Force
A force that moves through another force's combat positions during a passage of lines operation.

Forward Passage of Lines
A passage of lines occurring when a unit passes through another unit's positions while moving toward the enemy.

Passage Point
The specific point through which a passing force moves, where the transfer of authority usually occurs.

Supplies
Materials distributed to sustain land forces, which are deconflicted from troop movements by movement control.

Stationary Unit
A unit that occupies combat positions and through which another force passes during a passage of lines.

JP 3-18
A joint publication referenced as the source for the definition of passage of lines.

The Army
The military service that utilizes the term Area of Operations (AO) instead of a zone of operations.

Security Operation
An operation conducted to protect a force, which may necessitate a passage of lines.

AdministrativeMovement
The echelon logistic staff officer usually supervises administrative movements.

Combat Positions
Passage of lines involves a force moving through another force's combat positions.

22 FEB 2022
22 FEB 2022 is the publication date listed on the document header.<SEP>The publication date of the document ATP 3-06.1.<SEP>The publication date of the military manual ATP 3-06.1/MCRP 3-20.4/NTTP 3-01.04/AFTTP 3-2.29.<SEP>22 FEB 2022 is the publication date of the manual ATP 3-06.1/MCRP 3-20.4/NTTP 3-01.04/AFTTP 3-2.29.<SEP>The publication date associated with the military manual ATP 3-06.1/MCRP 3-20.4/NTTP 3-01.04/AFTTP 3-2.29.<SEP>The publication date associated with the military manual ATP 3-06.1.

MEDEVAC
Medical evacuation conducted using dedicated medical platforms protected by Geneva Conventions with en route care.

CASEVAC
Casualty evacuation conducted using general-mission aircraft without medical markings or specialized medical training.

Air Assault
Air Assaults engage enemy forces or seize key terrain using assault forces moved by rotary-wing or tiltrotor aircraft.<SEP>Military operation involving insertion of forces where enemy may identify potential LZs and emplace obstacles.

Air Movement
Operations using aircraft to move troops, equipment, and supplies to secured LZs using similar planning to air assault.

Personnel Recovery
Operations to recover isolated personnel in the urban environment, presenting multiple challenges.

Aircraft
Aircraft are used in urban environments for ISR and escort operations, with effectiveness influenced by altitude and terrain.<SEP>Vehicles including rotary-wing, tiltrotor, and fixed-wing assets used for air movement and evacuation.<SEP>Air vehicles used in urban operations that may require firing solutions for moving vehicles.

Ground Force Commander
The Ground Force Commander utilizes ISR data and tactical communication for dynamic decision making and mission adjustment.<SEP>Leader who decides on evacuation methods based on asset availability and medical personnel advice.

Geneva Conventions
International agreements that protect and mark dedicated medical platforms used in MEDEVAC.

JP 4-02
Joint Health Services publication referenced for more information on MEDEVAC and CASEVAC.

Structures
Buildings and constructions within the urban environment that provide cover for enemy forces and may be impacted by rotor wash.<SEP>Man-made buildings in urban environments that serve as targets or sources of debris and collateral damage.<SEP>Structures are used to mask firing locations and create challenges in identifying points of origin.

Isolated Personnel
Individuals in the urban environment who may have to stay relatively fixed due to evasion challenges.

Noncombatant Casualties
Individuals more likely to occur in urban settings, requiring commanders to be prepared to use evacuation assets.

Joint Health Services
The organization associated with JP 4-02, providing information on MEDEVAC and CASEVAC operations.

Patient Collection Points
Marked locations where patients are collected for evacuation, included in operational graphics for MEDEVAC and CASEVAC crews.

Fixed-Wing Aircraft
A type of aircraft involved in HA and DR operations requiring airspace control considerations.<SEP>Aircraft assets that require suitable landing areas like airfields to conduct air movement operations in urban environments.<SEP>Aircraft that complement rotary-wing platforms during targeting processes.

Rotor Wash
Airflow generated by rotorcraft that can create hazards by impacting loose debris and poorly constructed structures.

Ground Forces
Military units capable of identifying entrances and exits to subsurface sites.<SEP>Ground Forces normally use the surface as maneuver space and can identify entrances to subsurface sites.<SEP>Military units supported by precision fires and rapid troop movement from aviation operations.<SEP>Ground Forces are supported by aviation fires during combat operations.<SEP>Ground Forces are personnel operating in urban terrain who use marking devices and unconventional methods like spray paint.<SEP>Military units operating on the ground that request fire missions from aircraft.

Rotary-Wing Aircraft
Rotary-Wing Aircraft are used to move assault forces during air assaults.<SEP>A type of aircraft involved in HA and DR operations requiring airspace control considerations.<SEP>Aircraft assets vulnerable to ground fire from high points of observation in urban environments.<SEP>Aircraft capable of hovering and providing laser designation capability in urban environments.

JP 3-09.3
JP 3-09.3 is a joint publication referenced for information on aviation fires.<SEP>A reference document discussed in relation to post-launch aborts in urban environments.<SEP>A reference document providing information on post-launch aborts and buddy lasing procedures.

Rotary-wing Aircraft
Helicopters or similar aircraft preferred for running and diving fire techniques in urban terrain.

Running And Diving Fire
A preferred engagement technique in urban terrain due to increased weapons accuracy.

Hovering Fire
A tactic that exposes aircraft to small-arms fire and is only executed if essential.

Manned-unmanned Teaming
A compatible aircraft configuration that considers using unmanned systems for reconnaissance.

Unmanned Systems
Systems used for reconnaissance of the objective area to increase situational awareness.

Aerial Sniper Platform
A method employing snipers from rotary-wing aircraft for operational flexibility in CD-sensitive environments.

Sniper Teams
Units that may find ground missions not feasible and use aerial platforms for positioning.

Illumination Rounds
Ammunition used to provide light for night operations and target marking.<SEP>Deployable munitions that can cause collateral damage along with delivery components.

SEAD
Suppression of Enemy Air Defenses, provided by artillery to protect against surface-to-air threats.

Standoff Weapons
Long-range weapons requiring coordination for target location and fusing options.

JTACs
JTACs work with aircrews to vary flight paths and use FMV to confirm targets.<SEP>Joint Terminal Attack Controllers who coordinate standoff weapons and SEAD missions with aircrews.

GPS Receivers
Equipment that may experience jamming or spoofing, affecting targeting accuracy.

United States (US) Forces
Military forces whose ROE and friendly fire reduction techniques may be exploited by enemy forces.

Urban Camouflage
Camouflage techniques involving geometric patterns or improvised materials for urban settings.

Camouflage Paints
Materials evolved to blend protected targets with terrain or vegetation.

Camouflage Nets
Equipment including multispectral nets used for urban camouflage.

Night Vision Devices (NVDs)
Equipment used by aircrews that can be negatively impacted by smoke and fires from illumination rounds.

Observers
Personnel involved in coordinating details of SEAD missions.

Fire Support Coordinators
Personnel responsible for coordinating SEAD missions among aircrews and JTACs.

Target Marking
A purpose of indirect fires and illumination rounds to identify targets for aircrews.

CD
CD risks are increased in urban environments and must be minimized during operations.<SEP>Collateral Damage, which has an increased chance in urban environments due to population density.

SA
SA refers to Situational Awareness, which is increased by battle-tracking capabilities and control measures.<SEP>Situational Awareness, which is increased by using unmanned systems for reconnaissance.

ROE
ROE resolutions may need to be determined independently by aircrews during air interdiction missions.<SEP>Rules of Engagement, which enemy forces may attempt to exploit.

JIPOE
Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment, which determines the effectiveness of illumination rounds.

Post-launch Aborts
A procedure that may not be possible in urban environments, referenced in JP 3-09.3.

Military Transport Trucks
Military transport trucks are vehicles that may be disguised with commercial logos and false skins.<SEP>Vehicles used by other nations that may depict commercial product logos and advertising.

LZ
Landing Zone, where indirect fires provide pre-assault fires for occupation.

Surface-to-air Threats
Threats against which artillery provides effective SEAD fires for protection.

Civilian Casualty
A potential risk increased by lack of visibility when using standoff weapons.

Small-arms Fire
A threat that exposes hovering aircraft in urban environments.

Friendly Fire
Incidents where friendly forces are mistakenly engaged, increased by urban operation conditions like close quarters and identification problems.<SEP>A risk reduced by specific techniques employed by United States forces.

Collateral Objects
Objects in proximity to targets where location error must be minimized.

Munitions
Explosive or nonexplosive rounds delivered via aerial or direct fire, subject to impact angles and fuzing options.

Personnel
Includes friendly, civilian, and enemy individuals whose safety and movement are affected by weapon effects and operational hazards.

Weapons
Tools fired in or at structures that may penetrate walls and endanger adjacent structures.<SEP>Weapons capable of creating penetrating effects should be considered when engaging subsurface targets.<SEP>Tools favored for use in factories due to large windows and open interiors.<SEP>Tools used to engage targets, selected based on desired effects and collateral damage concerns in urban operations.

Collateral Damage
Damage that planners can help reduce by identifying population variances throughout the day.<SEP>Collateral Damage (CD) concerns are mitigated by quick analysis from intelligence analysts or airborne sensor operators.<SEP>Unintended damage to noncombatants and property resulting from military engagements, a primary concern in urban environments.

Lasing
A technique using laser designators to guide missiles, susceptible to environmental interference such as backscatter and reflective surfaces.

Debris
Remnants from destroyed targets, including glass shards and falling material, posing hazards to personnel and movement.

Missile
A guided weapon that tracks laser energy or other designations to strike intended targets.

Communication
Organized and clear exchange of information critical for preventing friendly fire incidents during operations.

Friendly Force Trackers
Devices used to identify the location of friendly forces, subject to limitations like interference and latency.

Blast Effects
Weapon effects creating high concern for collateral damage to surrounding structures due to overpressure and force.

Laser Designator
A device emitting laser energy to mark targets, potentially becoming a target itself due to visibility in urban environments.<SEP>A device used to mark targets with laser energy, requiring careful placement to mitigate reflection.

Reflective Surfaces
Surfaces in urban environments that can reflect laser energy to unintended locations during lasing techniques.<SEP>Materials like glass or polished metal that can return dangerous laser energy or cause tracking failures.

Shooter
Individuals engaging targets whose ability to observe round impact may be inhibited by smoke, dust, and shadows.

Observer
Individuals responsible for battle damage assessment whose ability may be inhibited by environmental effects.

Noncombatants
Civilians accommodated within the city alongside businesses and government functions.<SEP>Individuals not involved in fighting that operators must distinguish from combatants.<SEP>Civilian personnel protected from collateral damage during military engagements.

Smoke
Environmental factor that limits the capabilities of available sensors during acquisition.<SEP>Smoke is a marking device that presents challenges and could be poor for use in urban environments.<SEP>Environmental condition in urban areas that masks targets and inhibits observation.

Shadows
Lighting conditions in urban areas that mask targets and inhibit observation.

Fragmentation Effects
Weapon effects posing the highest risk to personnel but less damage to structures.

Dust
Environmental factor that limits the capabilities of available sensors during acquisition.<SEP>Environmental condition in urban areas that masks targets and inhibits observation.

Cratering Effects
Weapon effects that can prevent future use of infrastructure.

Flechette Rockets
Deployable munitions that can cause collateral damage along with delivery components.

Incendiary Effects
Weapon effects causing structural weakening and potential building collapse or fire spread.

Cluster Bomb Units
Deployable munitions that can cause collateral damage along with delivery components.

Glass Shards
Debris resulting from blast effects that cause significant hazards and injuries to noncombatant personnel.

Rural Environments
Contrasted with urban environments regarding concerns about laser designator visibility.

An illustration referenced regarding laser designation reflection considerations and mitigation techniques.<SEP>Reference material illustrating techniques to mitigate laser designation concerns on reflective surfaces.

Aviation Operations

Urban Environment
The Urban Environment is defined as a topographically complex operational setting where man-made construction and population density are the dominant features. This setting comprises urbanized areas containing streets, roads, buildings, open spaces, and vertical structures characterized by hard, smooth surfaces and reflective materials. The physical landscape is further defined by significant density that creates clutter and urban canyons, establishing a distinct backdrop for military operations.

Within this environment, military operations face unique tactical challenges driven by electromagnetic interference affecting military tools, as well as factors such as light, heat, and verticality that affect visibility and communication. The density and structures restrict ground movement and complicate air operations, while hard surfaces and reflective structures challenge weapon effects, movement, and weapon delivery. These physical constraints necessitate close-quarters engagements and create specific difficulties regarding orientation.

The Urban Environment presents increased risks for aviation and complicates target identification due to the complex setting. Operational complexities include difficulty in distinguishing friendly forces amidst the population density and infrastructure. Ultimately, the combination of these environmental factors creates a setting that significantly impacts military effectiveness, safety, and tactical execution across all domains.

Army Special Operations Forces are primary U.S. Army military units discussed in FM 3-05 responsible for conducting special operations activities across a spectrum of strategic contexts, including competition, crisis, and armed conflict. These forces transition between these contexts to achieve policy goals, maintain stability, and deter conflict through flexible response or deterrence operations. During crises, they act to counter provocation, deter escalation, and resolve threats, while also participating in stability operations and transitions back to competition. Their role encompasses conducting operations throughout the operational framework in armed conflict to support broader national objectives.

In terms of operational execution, Army Special Operations Forces operate in rear, close, and deep areas to support conventional forces and contribute to large-scale combat operations. They serve as a primary military organization conducting operations in deep areas to support joint force objectives and disrupt enemy capabilities. By working with partners to add operational depth, they support conventional operations while maintaining the ability to disrupt enemy cohesion. This is achieved by targeting systems that enable enemy situational awareness and coordinated action, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of the joint force during conflict.

Furthermore, Army Special Operations Forces engage deeply with local partners and understand partner nation culture to facilitate cooperation. They provide stay behind forces when necessary and work collaboratively to ensure operational success. Their activities are designed to add operational depth and support the broader joint force objectives during armed conflict and other strategic phases. The document details Army Special Operations Forces capabilities and operational conduct during competition, crisis, and armed conflict. As a publication dated 26 June 2025, it provides comprehensive text on the doctrines governing special operations.

The manual contains specific doctrine regarding security assistance and stability tasks, documenting the full range of Army Special Operations Forces responsibilities. While one description characterizes FM 3-05 as a Field Manual chapter discussing Special Operations During Armed Conflict, the majority identify it as the standalone manual detailing these forces during competition, crisis, and armed conflict. The document integrates guidance on activities during competition and conflict, ensuring clarity on Army Special Operations Forces doctrine. United States Army
The United States Army serves as the primary military branch operating armored and aviation assets, functioning as the overarching organization for acquisition, deployment, and sustainment of described weapon systems. It utilizes the Abrams tank as its primary ground combat system and oversees programs such as the Armored Multi-Purpose Vehicle (AMPV) and Integrated Air and Missile Defense (IAMd). The branch sets modernization priorities including Future Vertical Lift, Long-Range Precision Fires, Soldier Lethality, and the Army Network, managing projects from Acquisition Life Cycle phases to fleet lethality enhancements.

Operational capabilities encompass a wide range of vehicles and systems. Ground mobility involves the Family of Medium Tactical Vehicles (FMTV), Stryker program for rapid deployability, High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicles (HMMWV), Heavy Expanded Mobility Tactical Trucks (HEMTT), the PLSA1 fleet, and Utility Helicopter (UH-72A) for homeland defense. Protection and recovery are ensured through Mine Resistant Ambush Protected (MRAP) vehicles and the M88A2 Improved Recovery Vehicle. Combat firepower includes the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS), Multiple Launch Rocket System (MLRS), Paladin, M109A7 Self-Propelled Howitzer, and Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System (GMLRS). Missiles operated or procured include the Javelin, Joint Air-to-Ground Missile (JAGM), TOW, and Excalibur Projectile. Air assets involve helicopters and the MQ-1C Gray Eagle drone.

Technical infrastructure supports these operations through the Distributed Common Ground System-Army (DCGS-A) for intelligence and sensor tasking, alongside networking tactical radio systems. Administrative and logistical management relies on the General Fund Enterprise Business System (GFEBS) and Integrated Personnel and Pay System-Army (IPPS-A). The United States Army holds milestone authority for the Phased Array Tracking Radar and Intercept System (PAC-3) and operates the PATRIOT system, ensuring continuous implementation of upgrades to operational forces across all described domains.

Redstone Arsenal is a significant military installation located in Alabama that serves as a central hub for United States Army acquisition and modernization efforts. The facility functions as both a base and headquarters for two major executive offices: the Program Executive Office Aviation (PEO Aviation) and the Program Executive Office Missiles and Space (PEO Missiles and Space). As a primary location for these organizations, Redstone Arsenal hosts their respective operations and manages various defense modernization programs essential to national security infrastructure.

Within its scope of aviation oversight, Redstone Arsenal is the location associated with PEO Aviation operations and the management of Future Vertical Lift initiatives. The site is also linked to the administration of specific aerial systems, notably the RQ-7Bv2 Shadow system. These responsibilities highlight the arsenal's integral role in advancing aviation technologies and maintaining readiness through dedicated program management within the PEO Aviation framework.

Concurrently, regarding PEO Missiles and Space, Redstone Arsenal acts as the headquarters and operational location responsible for Integrated Air and Missile Defense (IAMD) activities. The facility oversees a diverse portfolio of programs, including the management of the PAC-3 program, the AN/TPQ-53 program, and handling HIMARS description specifications. Furthermore, the arsenal provides critical oversight for unmanned systems and rocketry, specifically the MQ-1C Gray Eagle and the Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System (GMLRS). Through these combined functions, Redstone Arsenal stands as a pivotal site for the development, specification, and management of critical defense assets across both aviation and missile domains.

Army Network is a designated modernization priority area identified by the United States Army for long-range improvement. This strategic initiative focuses specifically on communication and information infrastructure, aiming to modernize Army communications and network infrastructure to ensure effective operations. Future Vertical Lift
Future Vertical Lift, often abbreviated as FVL, is a designated modernization priority area explicitly identified by the United States Army. As one of the six core modernization priorities established for long-range improvement, it operates within the Army’s acquisition strategy and the TACA Modernization framework. The initiative is fundamentally defined as a strategic focus on next-generation rotary-wing aviation capabilities, aiming to enhance vertical mobility and ensure effective coordination with ground assets. Its primary objective is to improve aerial mobility and provide essential support for warfighters through a family of vertical lift solutions.

The program targets the delivery of these next-generation capabilities by 2030 and acts as a priority category supporting various aerial mobility assets, such as the CH-47F Chinook.
